title: A Leaked Memo Ties Cyberattacks on Minnesota Water Utilities to Iran
gist: A leaked WaterISAC memo is the first official document tying the wave of cyberattacks on more than 30 Minnesota water and wastewater utilities to Iran, citing a Minnesota Fusion Center alert that aligns the intrusions with a CISA-described 'Iran-affiliated' PLC-targeting campaign. Researchers split on whether CyberAv3ngers or Handala did it but agree on Iranian attribution, and warn this is the widest state-sponsored sabotage of US civilian infrastructure since the US-Iran war began in late February.

insights.claim: A leaked WaterISAC memo is the first official document explicitly linking the Minnesota water utility cyberattacks to Iran, relaying a Minnesota Fusion Center finding that the intrusions were 'aligned' with an April CISA campaign attributed to Iran-affiliated hackers.
insights.speaker: Andy Greenberg
insights.so_what: Formal attribution to a state actor is the trigger for federal response, sanctions, and mandated OT security spending across the water sector.
insights.quote: regarding ongoing malicious cyber activity impacting public drinking water systems across Minnesota
insights.locator: The WaterISAC note states that the Minnesota Fusion Center

insights.claim: Researchers disagree on which Iranian group is responsible — Tenable points to IRGC-linked CyberAv3ngers based on operational pattern, while Claroty found evidence pointing to Handala — but converge on Iranian state-linked actors.
insights.speaker: Andy Greenberg
insights.so_what: Group-level ambiguity does not blunt the policy consequence; treat state attribution as settled and group attribution as noise when handicapping escalation.
insights.quote: but in a very high likelihood we can say it’s Iranian actors

insights.claim: No Iranian hacker group has claimed responsibility and no official confirmation exists, and the updated CISA advisory still does not mention the Minnesota attacks — only the July 22 timing of its update suggests the connection.
insights.speaker: Andy Greenberg
insights.so_what: Official channels are lagging the leak, so market-moving confirmation is likely still ahead rather than priced.
insights.locator: The updated advisory, however, still doesn’t mention the Minnesota attacks

insights.claim: WaterISAC publicly distanced itself from the leak, saying it did not provide the memo to WIRED and did not assess attribution at any time.
insights.speaker: Andy Greenberg
insights.so_what: Information-sharing bodies retreating from attribution slows the sector-wide warning loop that utilities depend on.
insights.quote: WaterISAC always maintains information sharing protocols and safeguards information shared by our members, partners and the broader information sharing community
insights.locator: WaterISAC’s director of infrastructure cyber defense

themes.theme: Escalation in the US-Iran cyber conflict

insights.claim: Since the US launched its war against Iran in late February, Iranian hackers have retaliated by paralyzing medical supplies company Stryker and breaching FBI director Kash Patel's personal email, with the Minnesota water attacks the widest and most disruptive strike yet.
insights.speaker: Andy Greenberg
insights.so_what: Iranian cyber retaliation is escalating in severity along a visible ladder — corporate disruption, then official espionage, now physical-process sabotage.
insights.quote: the widest and most disruptive strike yet inflicted by the country’s hackers against the US since the war began
insights.locator: Since the US launched its war against Iran in late February

insights.claim: Documented disruption and modification of safety and protection parameters in critical infrastructure represents a tradecraft rarely seen outside Russia's war against Ukraine, and its spread to Iran across multiple sites marks a threshold change.
insights.speaker: Andy Greenberg
insights.so_what: A second state actor willing to sabotage civilian OT expands the threat model for every US utility, water, power, and gas operator.
insights.quote: Now we have documented disruption and even modification of safety and protection parameters in critical infrastructure
insights.locator: Confirmation of Iran’s responsibility for hacking the water utilities

insights.claim: The same targeted technology is deployed at many other sites, so the campaign has no structural reason to stop at Minnesota.
insights.speaker: Andy Greenberg
insights.so_what: Expect follow-on incidents in other states; the exposure is a technology monoculture, not a local lapse.
insights.quote: There are plenty of other sites that have the same targeted technology

themes.theme: PLC attack surface in water utilities

insights.claim: The attackers compromised remotely accessible programmable logic controllers with the likely desired impact of causing loss of system pressure and potential contamination of the water supply, per the Minnesota Fusion Center.
insights.speaker: Andy Greenberg
insights.so_what: Internet-exposed PLCs are the single named entry point — the remediation market and any compliance mandate will center on them.
insights.quote: with the likely desired impact to cause loss of system pressure and potential contamination of the water supply
insights.locator: The WaterISAC memo states that, according to the Minnesota Fusion Center

insights.claim: A new CISA advisory warns that the threat actors are targeting water entities of all sizes and instructs utilities to disconnect PLCs from the internet, password-protect access with strong passwords, and allow-list only trusted devices.
insights.speaker: Andy Greenberg
insights.so_what: Small municipal systems with no security staff are explicitly in scope, implying federal funding pressure and a long tail of remediation demand.
insights.quote: these threat actors are targeting water entities of all sizes
insights.locator: A new CISA advisory related to the attacks released Thursday

insights.claim: The attackers were exfiltrating and manipulating the project files that govern automated industrial systems, and earlier Iranian activity tampered with PLCs to change information on industrial control system displays.
insights.speaker: Andy Greenberg
insights.so_what: Manipulating configuration and display data means operators can be blinded before physical damage occurs — detection has to sit below the HMI layer.
insights.quote: In a few cases, this activity has resulted in operational disruption and financial loss
insights.locator: The CISA advisory that was updated last week

insights.claim: More than 30 Minnesota municipal water and wastewater systems were targeted, with breaches in some cases disabling telecommunications between industrial control system technologies and water utility equipment.
insights.speaker: Andy Greenberg
insights.so_what: A 30-plus-site simultaneous compromise indicates campaign-scale automation, not opportunistic single-target intrusion.
insights.quote: more than 30 municipal water and wastewater systems had been targeted
insights.locator: Earlier this week, Minnesota state officials revealed

insights.claim: The hacking briefly knocked out the water plant in the 1,700-person city of Braham and produced boil-water notices and sustained manual operations, but there is no evidence yet of water shortages or a threat to the safety of Minnesota's water supply.
insights.speaker: Andy Greenberg
insights.so_what: Physical consequence so far is degraded service rather than harm — the gap between capability demonstrated and damage inflicted is the escalation headroom to watch.
insights.locator: In at least one municipality, the 1,700-person city of Braham

insights.claim: Targeted municipalities emphasize that failsafes held: South St. Paul said contingency procedures let Public Works staff maintain normal water and wastewater operations despite affected automated controls.
insights.speaker: Andy Greenberg
insights.so_what: Manual fallback capability is the effective mitigation today, which argues against fully automating utility operations without staffed redundancy.
insights.quote: While the incident affected certain automated controls, established contingency procedures were immediately implemented, allowing Public Works staff to maintain normal water and wastewater operations
insights.locator: In the wake of the cyberattacks earlier this week

themes.theme: CyberAv3ngers track record and failed deterrence

insights.claim: CyberAv3ngers emerged in late 2023 after the October 7 Hamas attacks by targeting Unitronics industrial control devices used in water facilities, rewriting the devices' code and disrupting water services from Israel to Ireland to a US facility in Pittsburgh.
insights.speaker: Andy Greenberg
insights.so_what: The group has a multi-year, multi-country record against a specific vendor class — asset owners running that gear are the identifiable next targets.
insights.quote: the hackers had in fact rewritten the Unitronics’ devices’ code
insights.locator: In that first wave of cyberattacks, CyberAv3ngers targeted devices

insights.claim: A $10 million State Department bounty and Treasury sanctions on six IRGC officials failed to deter CyberAv3ngers, whose attacks escalated to breaching a US oil and gas company in 2024 and spreading IOControl malware across industrial control and IoT devices.
insights.speaker: Andy Greenberg
insights.so_what: Financial and legal deterrence has an empirically poor record against IRGC-linked crews, so defense spending — not sanctions headlines — is the operative response.
insights.locator: Even after the US State Department offered a $10 million bounty

insights.claim: CyberAv3ngers is a rare state-sponsored group willing not just to target but to sabotage industrial control systems, and water in particular, with both the capability and the intent to shut things off and potentially cause harm.
insights.speaker: Andy Greenberg
insights.so_what: Intent plus demonstrated capability against water systems is the profile that justifies pricing in a tail event for municipal utilities and their insurers.
insights.quote: They definitely have the capability; they have the intent
insights.locator: Dragos cybersecurity researcher Kyle O’Meara told WIRED
